title: Ipu Hula (gourd drum)

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Crosby Brown Collection of Musical Instruments, 1889
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A tall gourd drum from Hawai'i, about thirty inches high, made from gourd with tapa barkcloth and breadfruit gum.

context: An ipu hula, a gourd drum used to accompany hula, made in Hawai'i in the 19th century from gourd, tapa cloth, and breadfruit gum. It stands about 76 centimeters (30 inches) tall. Tapa is cloth made from the inner bark of trees.

descriptions.k: This is a drum made from a gourd, a hard-shelled plant. It is tall. People in Hawai'i used drums like this to make music for hula dance. Can you imagine the sound it makes?
descriptions.g12: This drum is called an ipu hula. It comes from Hawai'i and is made from a gourd, a plant with a hard shell. Tapa cloth and a sticky tree gum are also part of it. Drums like this help keep the beat for hula. How might it sound?
descriptions.g35: An ipu hula is a gourd drum made in Hawai'i to accompany hula, the dance of the islands. This one, from the 19th century, is about 76 centimeters tall and made from gourd, tapa cloth, and breadfruit gum. Tapa is a cloth made from tree bark. Look at how natural materials were joined into one instrument. Why might gourds make good drums?
descriptions.g68: The ipu hula is a gourd drum used in Hawai'i to keep rhythm for hula and chant. This 19th-century example is made of gourd, tapa cloth, and breadfruit gum, all natural materials from the islands. Its tall, rounded shape is both practical and elegant, and tapa, a bark cloth, shows that musical instruments could combine several crafts. The record gives the materials but not the maker, so what we see is a record of skill rather than a named artist.
descriptions.g910: The ipu hula joins several Hawaiian crafts: a gourd shaped for resonance, tapa cloth, and breadfruit gum used as an adhesive or sealant. Made in the 19th century, it accompanied hula and chant, in which rhythm and voice work with movement. The classification as an instrument may hide the object's sculptural qualities: its tall silhouette and natural materials form a unified design. How does an object designed for sound also work as a visual form?
descriptions.g1112: This ipu hula, a 19th-century gourd drum from Hawai'i, shows the interplay of material, sound, and performance. Gourd provides the resonating body, while tapa and breadfruit gum, an adhesive material, reflect the integrated use of local resources. Because hula is a living tradition, the instrument cannot be reduced to a museum object: its meaning lies partly in performance and community knowledge that the record does not capture. How should we describe an instrument when the sound that defines it is absent?

teacherNote.context: The ipu hula is a gourd drum used to accompany hula in Hawai'i. This 19th-century example is made of gourd, tapa cloth, and breadfruit gum and is about 30 inches tall; hula remains a living tradition.
directions: Have students make a rhythm with household objects and compare how shape affects sound.
Ask students to explore how tapa (barkcloth) is made from tree bark.
Invite students to watch or listen to a performance of hula with permission from a trusted source and discuss the role of the drum.
